question: Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 requires producers in the EU, such as JSW, to measure and report methane emissions and to comply with limits on its release. Importers of oil, gas and coal, such as ORLEN and Węglokoks, must obtain documentation from foreign producers, report emissions and demonstrate the equivalence of their emission measurement and verification systems.

These obligations incur costs, and failure to comply with them may result in penalties. On 20 July 2026, the Commission recommended that certain penalties not be imposed on importers between 2027 and 2029. On 6 October 2026, it announced an additional year of flexibility for foreign suppliers. By 5 August 2027, the Commission is to set emission limits for ventilation shafts in coking coal mines.

JSW is the only producer in the EU of high-quality coking coal, recognised by the EU as a critical raw material in Regulation (EU) 2024/1252. The coke produced from it is used in steel production, including for the defence industry. 1.

Will the Commission propose exempting coking coal mines from methane emission limits in order to protect the extraction of a raw material that is critical to the European steel and defence industries?

What are the Commission’s estimates of the costs of compliance with the new obligations for importers such as ORLEN and Węglokoks, and if no such estimates have been drawn up, why were the provisions adopted without specifying them?
How will the Commission ensure that future restrictions do not force JSW to reduce its production and do not increase the European steel industry’s dependence on imports?
